sections.h2: Which offices handle property tax in Mecosta County?
sections.html:
Property tax here passes through four desks, and each answers a separate question. The local assessor puts a value on the house. The township or city treasurer mails the first bill and takes the first payment. Equalization at the county tests whether each unit values property evenly. The county treasurer inherits whatever is still unpaid on March 1.

The Equalization Department, reachable at (231) 592-0108, does not set an individual owner's assessment. It studies whole property classes in the county's 16 townships and one city so the Board of Commissioners can equalize each class to 50 percent of true cash value. Its page also carries the annual millage rates, the apportionment report, a property tax estimator and a list of township assessors.

The county treasurer's page sends owners to Equalization at the same number for name and address changes. Owners in a village receive two bills in July, one from the township and one from the village, and each is paid to its own treasurer.

sections.h2: What are the Mecosta County property tax due dates?
sections.html:
Bills for the summer levy are mailed in the first week of July and can be paid without penalty through September 14. The winter bill follows in December. The county treasurer's page quotes MCL 211.44(2): a bill that is lost or never received does not cancel the tax, so ask the township, city or village if nothing arrives.

Mecosta County billing and delinquency timeline from the county treasurer's page
WhenWhat happens
Early JulySummer bills mailed by the township, city or village
September 14Last day for the summer bill without interest
After September 14Interest of 1 percent per month
DecemberWinter bill issued
After February 14Townships may add 3 percent until February 28
March 1Unpaid taxes turn delinquent and go to the county treasurer

After March 1 the county treasurer adds a 4 percent administration charge and runs interest at 1 percent a month. A full year of delinquency means forfeiture, at which point interest jumps to 1.5 percent a month, counted back to the day the taxes first went delinquent.

sections.h2: What happens if property taxes go unpaid in Mecosta County?
sections.html:
The path runs through forfeiture to foreclosure. Roughly 23 months of delinquency ends in foreclosure, with title moving to the State of Michigan, because the state serves as Mecosta County's foreclosing governmental unit. The state auctions the parcel, and the sale results appear on Tax-Sale.info.

When an auction brings in more than what was owed, the former owner may claim the surplus. The county treasurer's page walks through the steps: file Form 5743 with the state by the July 1 after the foreclosure date, wait for the state's response, then ask the circuit court for payment between February 1 and May 15. The separate window for pre-2021 sales closed March 31, 2025.

For anyone a few months behind, March 1 is the date to beat. Ask the treasurer for a payoff figure and, if you plan to sell, close before the parcel hits forfeiture.

sections.h2: How does a sale change the taxes on a Mecosta County house?
sections.html:
A sale usually raises the taxable value. Year over year, taxable value may rise by no more than 5 percent or the inflation rate, whichever is less, but a change of ownership removes that limit and sets taxable value equal to the state equalized value the next year (MCL 211.27a). A long-time owner's bill can therefore look quite different on the buyer's first statement.

Some changes of hands leave the cap alone, among them transfers between spouses, certain residential transfers to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild who will not use the property commercially, and a foreclosure until the lender resells. The new owner has 45 days to tell the assessor, and the Property Transfer Affidavit is on the county's Equalization forms page as Form 2766.

Sellers who claimed the principal residence exemption should withdraw it after they move. The same page offers Form 2602 for that request and Form 2368 for the buyer's homestead affidavit. Farmland owners will also find the farmland exemption claim (Form 2599) and the qualified agricultural property affidavit (Form 3676) there.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Mecosta County assessment?
sections.html:
Begin at the Board of Review in your township or city, which meets the week of the second Monday in March (MCL 211.30). The week must include at least 12 hours of sessions, some after 6 p.m. You may protest in person, send an agent, or write a letter where the local unit has allowed that.

The board owes written notice of its decision by the first Monday in June. An owner who still disagrees can petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal: July 31 of the tax year for residential and agricultural property, May 31 for commercial and industrial (MCL 205.735a). A residential owner generally must have protested to the Board of Review first.

Questions about one assessment go to the township hall, and the Equalization page keeps a list of township assessors. Four townships publish hall details on the county's township page:

  • Colfax, hall at 14428 157th Ave., meets the third Wednesday at 6 p.m.
  • Grant, hall at 14982 21 Mile Rd., meets the second Monday at 6:30 p.m.
  • Hinton, hall at 9013 3 Mile Rd., Lakeview, meets the second Monday at 7 p.m.
  • Millbrook, hall at 3015 Jackson Rd., Blanchard, meets the first Monday at 7 p.m. and keeps office hours by appointment

The villages of Mecosta and Stanwood meet the first Monday at 6 p.m. and the second Monday at 7 p.m. respectively. The rest of the townships maintain their own websites.

sections.h2: What do Mecosta County property taxes mean for a seller at closing?
sections.html:
Closing usually includes a proration of the current bill, and for a warranty deed the county treasurer must certify that five years of taxes are paid (MCL 211.135). Afterward the register of deeds in Big Rapids records the deed and the assessors learn of the transfer.

The federal survey for 2020 to 2024 reports a typical house value of $178,900, monthly owner costs of $1,293 with a mortgage and $480 without, and household income near $60,951. Those numbers hint at what a buyer can carry, though the real bill turns on the township, village and school district millage on each parcel.

  • Ask the township or city treasurer for the current balance, and the county treasurer for any delinquent amount.
  • Find the parcel's millage in the county's published millage rates for the year.
  • Rescind any principal residence exemption after the sale.
  • Give the buyer the date by which the transfer affidavit is due.

faqs.q: What is the deadline for the summer tax bill in Mecosta County?
faqs.a: September 14 is the last penalty-free day. Winter bills follow in December, and after February 14 townships may add 3 percent through the end of that month. March 1 sends anything unpaid to the county treasurer.

faqs.q: What does a late Mecosta County bill cost?
faqs.a: Interest of 1 percent a month starts after September 14 on the summer bill. At the county treasurer, a 4 percent administration charge is added, and interest climbs to 1.5 percent a month after forfeiture.

faqs.q: When does Mecosta County property reach tax foreclosure?
faqs.a: After roughly 23 months of delinquency. Forfeiture comes after the first year, and the State of Michigan then auctions the foreclosed parcel.

faqs.q: Does the county or my township decide what my Mecosta County house is worth?
faqs.a: The township or city assessor decides it. Equalization at the county measures whether each unit assesses at 50 percent of true cash value but does not value individual homes.

faqs.q: Is there a way to recover surplus from a Mecosta County tax sale?
faqs.a: Yes, when the auction price exceeds the debt. File Form 5743 by July 1 after the foreclosure date, then make a circuit court motion between February 1 and May 15.
